gap: No result ChatGPT got states why a 2.4 GHz keyboard dongle drops or delays keys next to a USB 3.0 port (USB 3.0 signalling puts broadband noise in the 2.4-2.5 GHz band the dongle listens on) or the fix the makers give: put the receiver on a USB 2.0 extension, about 12 in (30 cm) from the PC case and any USB 3.0 cable.
standout_why: Compared against the two cited pages (techgearden.com, kazsushibistro.com) and four uncited results (keebkit.com, gearedgaming.com, keebscout.com, primeareviews.com). kazsushibistro has part of it: one anecdote that the AULA F99 dongle 'did not stutter even when my desk was crowded with USB 3.0 devices', plus general figures of 30-50 ms Bluetooth against 1-5 ms on 2.4 GHz. gearedgaming says Bluetooth 'occasionally drops the first keystroke after an idle period'. None names the 2.4-2.5 GHz overlap, the symptoms, or the extension-cable fix; techgearden, keebkit, keebscout and primeareviews say nothing on it.
decides: It does not change the pick, because every 2.4 GHz board in this price band is equally exposed; it decides whether the wireless half of the plan works on the shopper's desk and gives the fix. It confirms a tri-mode board over a Bluetooth-only one, since USB-C cable and Bluetooth remain as fallbacks. The Keychron J5 is the only candidate where I read a maker-stated 1,000 Hz polling rate and wireless N-key rollover. For the Gamakay TK101 (the one partner board with a number pad under $60), the store text I read never names a 2.4 GHz receiver, so check that before the page calls it a dongle board.

findings.label: Why a 2.4 GHz dongle stutters beside USB 3.0 (Attack Shark's own explanation)
findings.value: USB 3.0 noise 'overlaps directly with the 2.4GHz to 2.5GHz band used by wireless mice, keyboards, and Wi-Fi'; a USB 3.0 connector 'can add approximately 20dB of broadband noise to the 2.4GHz band'
findings.source_title: Eliminating 2.4GHz Stutter: Solving USB 3.0 Port Interference (Attack Shark, published 2025-12-28)
findings.note: Attack Shark makes the X98 candidate, but the article names no keyboard model. The 20 dB figure is Attack Shark citing Intel's white paper; I did not read it in Intel's paper itself. The noise lowers the receiver's signal-to-noise ratio and packets drop.

findings.label: Fix Attack Shark gives
findings.value: USB 2.0 extension cable (with ferrite choke) keeping the receiver at least 12 in (30 cm) from the PC case and any USB 3.0 cables
findings.source_title: Eliminating 2.4GHz Stutter: Solving USB 3.0 Port Interference (Attack Shark)
findings.note: The article adds that moving the dongle to a USB 2.0 port may not be enough if that port sits next to an active USB 3.0 port.

findings.label: Symptoms and fix in Logitech's words
findings.value: Symptoms: 'Delayed response to mouse or keyboard inputs', 'Missing keyboard characters or mouse commands', 'Decreased operating distance'. Fix: 'separate your USB 3.0 and USB 2.0 receivers by as much distance as possible', keep the receiver close to the keyboard, use an extender cable
findings.source_title: Wireless product not working properly when also using a USB 3.0 device (Logitech support)
findings.note: The page is undated (footer says © 2026). Logitech says a 2.4GHz device 'may experience erratic operation caused by interference' when a USB 3.0 device is connected; it does not explain the cause further.
